context: In general, the tripos-to-topos construction does not give a univalent category. A counter example for such a non-univalent category is the following. Every complete Heyting algebra H gives rise to a tripos such that the formulas on a set X are the same as functions X → H. If we apply the tripos-to-topos construction, then we get the category of H-valued sets [11]. If H is the terminal Heyting algebra, we obtain the category whose objects are sets but where each hom-set is the unit type – which is clearly not univalent. ▶ Example 11 (functor categories). Let A and C be categories. Univalence is preserved under taking functor categories. That is, if C is univalent, then the category [A, C] of functors is also univalent [2, Thm. 4.15]. However, it is not provable that the Rezk completion of a functor category [A, C] is (equivalent to) the functor category [A, RC(C)] for every A and C. That this is not provable follows from choosing A to be a discrete category on a set X, and C the 1-object category associated to the group Z/2. Then, from an equivalence between [A, RC(C)] and RC([A, C]) we can derive the statement: ! Y Y Y Y ∥P(x) ≃ 2∥ → ∥ P(x)∥. It remains an open problem whether the statement Q A,C RC([A, C]) ≃ [A, RC(C)] is consistent, and is hence independent from UF. A bicategorical perspective. To lift the Rezk completion from categories to structured categories, we formulate the Rezk completion bicategorically. Analogous to the way that structured sets, e.g., monoids, form the objects in their respective categories, categories with additional structure form the objects in a bicategory [1]. One advantage of working bicategorically is that we can treat structure uniformly. Furthermore, the universal property of the Rezk completion can be internalized in the bicategory Cat of categories, functors, and natural transformations, since the Rezk completion makes the bicategory Catuniv of univalent categories into a reflective subbicategory of Cat. That is, the inclusion of Catuniv into Cat has a left biadjoint (Proposition 13). ▶ Definition 12 ( ). Let R : B1 → B2 be a pseudofunctor. A left biadjoint L for R is given by: 1. a function L : B2 → B1 ; Q 2. a family of morphisms η : X:B2 X → R(L(X)) called the unit; such that for every X : B2 and Y : B1 , the functor ηX · R(−) : B1 (L X, Y ) → B2 (X, R Y ), is an adjoint equivalence of categories.
